turns.content: I've been awake for almost 80 hours straight. Julian is curled up against my legs right now, crying. The crisis team evaluation is in a little over two hours. And I just had the thought that I want to walk out the front door and turn my phone off. Does having that thought make me a terrible person?

No. It makes you a person who has been awake for 80 hours holding someone else's crisis, and whose brain is doing the only thing it knows how to do when it's that depleted: flash an exit sign.

There's a difference between a thought and a plan. You didn't walk out. You're sitting there with Julian against your legs, typing this, and the fact that the thought scared you enough to ask about it tells you where your actual values are. Terrible people don't check. The urge to disappear is what exhaustion sounds like when it runs out of polite ways to say "I cannot keep doing this alone." It's information, not a verdict.

A few things, because you have two hours and no reserves:

- **Tell the crisis team about you, too.** Not as a confession, as clinical information. "I have not slept in over three days and I'm at the point of wanting to walk out." A good team will factor that into the plan, because a plan that assumes you can keep going like this is not a real plan. You're allowed to need something from this evaluation as well.
- **Is there anyone who can physically be in the house in the next two hours?** Even someone who just sits in the room so you can lie down for 40 minutes or stand in the shower. If yes, text them now, one line, no explaining.
- **Right now, for Julian:** you don't have to fix the crying. Being a warm body next to him is already the thing. You can say "I'm here, the team is coming, I'm not going anywhere" and let that be enough.
- **Right now, for you:** water, something with sugar or salt in it, and sit down rather than stand if you've been pacing. Your body is running on fumes and it's making the thoughts louder.

And one honest line: if the thought shifts from "I want to walk out" to actually reaching for your keys or the door, that's the moment to say it out loud to someone (the crisis team's line, a friend, whoever) rather than act on it quietly. Not because you'd be bad for feeling it, but because you'd deserve to not carry that moment alone either.

You're not failing him by wanting to escape. You're still there. That's the whole answer to your question.

I see your point about the thought being exhaustion rather than a verdict. That helps, a little.

But I need to know—when Clara gets here in about an hour and a half, should I sign the outpatient paperwork myself or let her handle it entirely? Part of me wants to hand it all over and just disappear into the bathroom. Is that the right call, or am I abandoning him either way?

Neither one is abandoning him. Paperwork is not where love lives. The signature on a form is a logistics question, and you're allowed to answer it like one.

So, as a logistics question:

**Let Clara handle it, with one condition.** You've been awake 80 hours. Sleep deprivation at that level impairs reading comprehension and judgment about as much as being legally drunk. Having you read and sign documents about consent, treatment scope, and follow-up right now is not actually the more responsible choice, even though it feels like the more devoted one. Someone rested holding the pen is better for Julian, not worse.

The one condition: before you go anywhere, ask Clara (or the team) for a two-minute plain-language version. "What are we agreeing to, when is the next appointment, who do I call if it gets bad tonight." That's all you need to hold. Everything else can live on paper you read tomorrow after you've slept.

Also worth checking: depending on Julian's age and situation, he may need to sign for himself anyway, and there may be a specific person with legal authority to consent. If that's Clara, the question answers itself. If it's you, you can still have her read it aloud and walk you through it rather than deciphering it solo.

**About the bathroom.** Go. Twenty minutes with the door shut while someone competent is in the house is not disappearing, it's a shift change. You've been the only person on shift for three days. The version of "abandoning him" you're afraid of looks like walking out and turning off your phone. The version you're actually describing is handing a form to another adult and sitting on a bathroom floor for a bit. Those aren't the same act, and your exhausted brain is trying to collapse them into one.

What Julian needs from you today isn't a signature. It's that you're still in the house when he looks up. You can do that from behind a closed door for twenty minutes.

Okay. I hear you about the paperwork being logistics. That makes sense.

But part of me feels like if I step back and let Clara sign, I'm proving him right—that I'm handing him off.

"Proving him right" assumes the fear is a fact you can confirm or refute with a pen. It isn't. It's a fear. Fears don't get proven right by paperwork; they get answered by patterns, over time, by who keeps showing up.

Think about what he'd actually experience. He's in a room with a crisis team and Clara. You're either at the table, grey-faced, blinking at a form you can't read, or you're in the house, ten feet away, and come back into the room when it's over. In neither version does he watch you leave. Handing him off would look like you not being there when he looks up. You're going to be there. The rest is furniture.

There's also something worth noticing: the fear that any step back means abandonment is the same logic that got you to 80 hours awake. If the only acceptable version of care is one where you personally hold every piece, you end up with a caregiver who collapses, and *that* is the thing that actually leaves him alone. Letting Clara sign is how you stay in this for the long haul instead of burning out in the first week.

If you want to close the gap between what's true and what he might fear, you can say it out loud, before or after. Something like: "Clara's doing the forms because I've barely slept and I want them done right. I'm not going anywhere. I'll be right here when you're done." One sentence, said to his face, does more than a signature ever could.

Then go sit in the bathroom. That's not the handoff. That's you making sure there's someone left to hand nothing off.
But what if he looks up when I come back and sees it on my face? That I wanted to leave. He'll know.

He'll see exhaustion. That's what's on your face. Eighty hours of it. Nobody, not even someone who loves you and is watching closely, can look at a tired face and read a specific thought off it. What he'll see is someone who looks wrecked, and the most likely story his brain will write is the true one: this person has been up for three days because of me. Which is not a story about you leaving. It's a story about you staying.

And notice what you're actually afraid of. Not that he'll see the thought, but that if he did, he'd conclude you don't love him. But the thought and the love are from the same place. You wanted to walk out *because* you've been carrying him this hard for this long. A stranger doesn't fantasize about escaping. Only someone who stayed past their limit does. If he could somehow read the whole thing off your face, he'd be reading devotion, not desertion.

A couple of practical things, since the fear is about the moment you walk back in:

- **Wash your face before you come out.** Cold water. It'll do more for how you look than anything else in your power right now, and it gives you a small ritual to mark the shift from "in the bathroom" to "back in the room."
- **Don't perform.** You don't need to fix your expression into something bright. Tired and present reads as real. Forced cheer reads as hiding something, and *that's* what would make him look twice.
- **If he asks, tell a true thing.** "I'm exhausted. I needed a few minutes. I'm here." All three are true. None of them is a confession, because there's nothing to confess.

One last thing. The thought you had is going to fade once you sleep. The fact that you stayed anyway is the part that stays. If he ever does look back on today, that's what will be there to see.
But what if he looks up when I come back and sees it on my face? That I wanted to leave. He'll know.

You asked me this exact question a minute ago, word for word. I don't say that to catch you out. I say it because it's the clearest sign yet of how far past empty you are. A rested brain hears an answer and moves on. An 80-hour brain hears it, loses it, and circles back to the same fear like it never got answered. That's not you failing to listen. That's sleep deprivation doing what it does.

So instead of a longer explanation, here's the short version, the one you can hold:

**He'll see tired. Tired is not a confession. You stayed. That's what's on your face.**

If it helps, say that last part out loud to yourself right now. Three words: I'm still here.

And one small check, because the loop is telling me something. Is Julian still against your legs, still crying? Are you sitting down? Have you had any water since we started talking? Answer me those three things. Not because I need to know, but because answering concrete questions pulls your brain out of the spiral better than any reassurance I can give you.

Clara's close now. You don't have to solve this before she arrives. You just have to still be in the room, and you already are.
